Welcome to a journey that's all about finding hope, healing, and new beginnings. Imagine this: what if every mistake you’ve made, every regret you carry, could lead you closer to something truly transformative? That’s the heart of what we’re about to explore together.
Through the pages of The Miracle of Forgiveness, Spencer W. Kimball invites us to take a closer look at the real power of forgiveness—how it can change us, heal us, and help us grow. We all wrestle with shortcomings and wish we could rewrite certain chapters of our lives. But here’s the incredible part: inside those struggles, there’s a chance to find peace and a genuine sense of renewal.
As we dive into the steps of repentance, honest self-reflection, and the courage it takes to truly change, we’ll see that forgiveness isn’t just a one-time event. It’s a process—a path that asks for humility, faith, and a willingness to believe that grace is within reach for everyone, no matter how far you feel you’ve fallen.
So, let’s set out together to discover what it really means to let go of guilt, embrace change, and move toward spiritual wholeness. There’s a powerful promise waiting ahead: lasting transformation, and the assurance that none of us are ever beyond the reach of hope.

Chapter 1: Recognizing the Weight of Mistakes and the Need for Change
You know, there comes a moment in almost everyone’s life when you realize—you’ve made a mistake. Sometimes, it sneaks up quietly, a little thought that just won’t leave you alone. Other times, it hits you all at once, like a heavy weight pressing on your heart. It’s rarely comfortable, but for many of us, that’s where the journey toward something better really begins.
Picture this: a young man, sitting alone after a heated argument with his family. The words he’d said keep echoing in his mind—harsher, more painful than he meant. He tries to shrug it off, but the guilt just lingers. It’s not just regret—it’s that deeper sense that something inside needs fixing. And honestly, that’s how the path toward forgiveness usually starts—with that uncomfortable truth that things aren’t as they should be.
Most of us, sooner or later, come face-to-face with our own flaws. Sometimes it’s little things—maybe cutting corners at work, snapping at a friend, or letting pride get in the way of kindness. Other times, it’s a bigger choice, one that leaves a mark you can’t ignore. The details are different for everyone, but the feeling is the same: you sense a distance from what’s right, and from the peace you really want.
In moments like that, it’s tempting to brush things aside. Maybe you distract yourself, hoping the feeling will just fade. Or you look at others and convince yourself, “Hey, at least I’m not as bad as them.” But deep down, you know when you’ve crossed a line. That discomfort? It’s a signal. A call to stop and ask: what needs to change?
We all know that everyone makes mistakes. What isn’t talked about as much is just how serious those mistakes can be, and the real consequences they bring. In Latter-day Saint teachings, sin isn’t just about breaking a rule—it’s about damaging your relationship with God. It’s turning away from what’s good, and it leaves you feeling spiritually distant.
There’s a woman who realized, looking back, that her choices had slowly pulled her away from things she once loved. She never meant to drift, but missing church now and then, skipping prayer, letting little grudges grow—it all built up. Eventually, she felt empty, and wishing things were different just wasn’t enough anymore. She saw that the road back would take more than hoping for change.
Now, recognizing the seriousness of a mistake isn’t about making you feel hopeless or ashamed. It’s about seeing what’s really at stake. Think about it—before a doctor can offer a cure, they have to admit there’s an illness, right? In the same way, you have to be honest about where you are before real healing can start. That honesty is the very first step toward change.
Some folks worry their mistakes are just too big to forgive. The thought of being beyond help can freeze you in your tracks. But here’s the heart of the gospel—it’s all about hope. No matter how far you’ve wandered, there’s always a way back. It’s not an easy road, and it takes more than a simple, “I’m sorry.” But it’s possible. And it all begins with the courage to see things as they really are.
So, the journey toward forgiveness? It starts with recognizing you need it. Not to drown in guilt, but to open the door to something better. That’s the foundation—where every real change begins.

Chapter Two: Understanding Repentance as a Lifelong Process
So, once you realize something in your life needs to change, you might wonder—what now?
Sometimes, we think of repentance as this big, dramatic moment. Maybe a tearful confession, a heartfelt prayer, or a promise to do better.
But you know, for most of us, real change looks a lot less like a lightning bolt, and a lot more like a slow sunrise—unfolding over days, months, maybe even years.
Picture a father who struggles with impatience. He finds himself snapping at his kids more often than he’d like. Each time, he regrets it—but the pattern keeps repeating.
It’s only when he starts to see repentance not as a one-time fix, but as a journey, that things begin to shift. He learns to pause, to apologize, and to try again. Not just once, but as many times as he needs.
Repentance, at its core, is about turning away from what’s wrong and moving toward what’s right.
Sure, feeling sorry is often part of it, but it’s much more than just regret. It’s a true change of heart and behavior—a shift in your priorities and what you really want.
Most of us find out pretty quickly that this isn’t something you do just once. Old habits have a way of sneaking back in. You might stumble and have to start again. But the secret? It’s all about persistence.
Let’s break down what real repentance looks like. First, you have to recognize there’s a problem—just being honest with yourself.
Then comes real sorrow, not just because you got caught or because things went badly, but because you see the hurt that’s been done.
After that, it’s confession. Admitting your mistake—to another person, or to God.
Next is restitution: making things right, as much as you can.
And finally, there’s the commitment to leave the old behavior behind.
Think of the college student who got caught cheating on an exam. Instead of hiding, she chose to come forward.
It wasn’t easy—admitting to her professor, facing consequences, and dealing with her family’s disappointment.
But through all of it, she found a sense of relief she didn’t expect. The burden of secrecy was gone, and she discovered the strength to rebuild her integrity.
A lot of people really struggle with confession. It can feel humiliating to admit when you’ve messed up—especially if it’s something big.
But here’s something to remember: confession isn’t about punishment. It’s about being honest.
It breaks the grip that secrecy and shame can have on you.
And more often than not, once you speak the truth out loud, the path forward becomes much clearer.
Restitution is tough, too. Sometimes, you can fix what’s broken—maybe you return something you took, apologize to someone you hurt, or do what you can to make things right.
Other times, the damage can’t be completely undone. But even then, the effort matters. It shows you’re sincere and you’re really committed to change.
And then there’s that last step—actually letting go of the old pattern. That’s often the hardest part. Old habits don’t disappear overnight, and temptation is always lurking.
But every time you choose differently, the past starts to lose its grip. New habits take root, and before you know it, the change becomes part of who you are.
So, here’s the key takeaway: repentance isn’t a punishment—it’s a gift.
It’s how you let go of what’s holding you back and move toward something better.
It takes humility, courage, and a lot of persistence.
But if you stick with it, you’ll find freedom—a sense of peace and hope that comes from knowing you’re on the right path.

Let’s talk about something we all wrestle with: The Dangers of Delay and the Power of Immediate Action.
You know how easy it is to push aside mistakes, right? Life gets hectic, and facing what’s gone wrong can feel like just too much. Maybe you’ve told yourself, “I’ll deal with it later,” hoping things will just work out on their own. But more often than not, waiting only makes things heavier—never lighter.
Picture a man in his middle years, carrying around a secret he made in his youth. He convinced himself it was too late to do anything about it. So, he built his life around dodging that uncomfortable truth. But the guilt? It never really went away. It wasn’t until a health scare forced him to face his own mortality that he finally reached out for forgiveness. The journey was tough, but he couldn’t help but wish he’d started sooner. All those years of hiding had stolen the peace he could’ve had all along.
Procrastination is sneaky. It whispers that there’s always tomorrow, that you can put off the pain of making things right. But if you’ve ever gone down that road, you probably know—it’s costly. The longer you leave a mistake untouched, the more it starts to shape your life. Relationships can suffer, your confidence can slip, and you might even feel a growing distance from God.
Some folks hope that time alone will heal old wounds. But here’s something to pay attention to—time, all by itself, doesn’t bring forgiveness. Real healing takes effort: you’ve got to recognize the problem, confess it, make things right, and then commit to change. The sooner you start, the sooner you’ll feel the weight begin to lift.
There’s another risk, too—getting a little too comfortable with the small mistakes. Take a teenager who starts telling harmless little lies to stay out of trouble. Over time, the lies come easier, and that twinge of guilt fades away. Before long, what started as a simple habit can become a pattern that’s tough to break. And it’s not just lying—anger, selfishness, even neglect can quietly weave themselves into our lives if we don’t address them.
But immediate action isn’t about panicking or trying to be perfect. It’s about tuning in to that quiet voice inside that says, “Hey, something here needs to change.” Most of us, deep down, know when we’re being nudged to do better. The real challenge? Listening—and acting, before the moment slips away.
Let me share one more story. There was a woman who’d held a grudge against her sibling for years. One day, she decided to pick up the phone. That first conversation was awkward, but as they talked, years of resentment started to melt away. She realized the hardest part was simply taking that first step. And once she did, the path ahead got so much clearer.
So, here’s the key takeaway: Don’t wait. The sooner you start making things right, the sooner you’ll experience the freedom and relief that forgiveness brings. Sure, you can’t change the past. But the future? That’s still wide open. Every single day is a fresh chance to begin again.

Chapter 4: The Transforming Power of Forgiveness and the Role of Christ’s Atonement.
Forgiveness—it’s not just about wiping away guilt. It’s a deep, life-changing transformation that can reach every corner of your heart. If you’ve ever carried the heavy weight of past mistakes, you know what it’s like to suddenly feel that burden lift. It’s like finally stepping out of a long, dark tunnel into the warmth and brightness of day. Relief, hope, and a new kind of strength all come rushing in.
Let me share a story that might sound familiar. There was a mother who spent years weighed down by regret over choices she’d made when she was younger. No matter how hard she worked or how much she tried to serve others, her pain wouldn’t budge. She kept it hidden, thinking maybe she could make up for her past. But nothing really changed, not until she decided to reach out for forgiveness—admitting her need, opening her heart in prayer, and letting others help. That’s when things started to shift. The real change wasn’t just in her daily life, but deep within her. She became more patient, more compassionate, and found a peace she hadn’t known in years.
Here’s something important to remember: forgiveness isn’t something you can just earn by racking up good deeds. It’s a gift. And for believers in Christ, it’s a gift made possible through His atonement. In Latter-day Saint faith, Christ’s sacrifice bridges the gap between where we are and who we can become. Every mistake—no matter how serious—can be overcome because of Him.
Now, I get it—this can be tough to accept, especially if you feel like you’re too far gone or just not good enough. Maybe you’ve wondered if forgiveness is really for you, or if you even deserve another chance. But here’s the heart of the gospel: nobody is beyond hope. Christ’s atonement is infinite. It covers every sin, every weakness, every setback. The only thing you need is a sincere desire to change, and a willingness to take those steps of repentance.
Of course, forgiveness isn’t always instant. Sometimes, echoes from past choices stick around, and the journey back can take time. But every single step—no matter how small—brings you closer to peace. When you start to feel forgiven, it changes not just your mood, but the way you see yourself and the world around you.
Let’s look at another example. There was a man who battled addiction for years. It took real courage for him to seek help. His road to recovery wasn’t easy—there were plenty of stumbles. But he kept going. And over time, he noticed something different: he was more patient with himself, more understanding with others, and he started to appreciate the little moments of happiness. The forgiveness he felt became his anchor, giving him the strength to keep moving forward, even on the hard days.
It’s not just individuals who are changed by forgiveness. Relationships can heal, too. When someone who’s been hurt decides to let go of resentment, it’s like unlocking a door for both people involved. Forgiving isn’t about pretending the hurt never happened. It’s about freeing yourself from the grip of anger and bitterness. That’s what opens the way for trust, reconciliation, and brand-new beginnings.
At the center of all this is the atonement of Christ. It’s the solid ground beneath every hope for change. Because of Him, you can find the strength to grow, the courage to face your mistakes, and the reassurance that you’re never alone in this process.
So, what’s the real miracle of forgiveness? It’s not just that your past can be wiped away. It’s that your whole life can be transformed.

Chapter Five: Living in Harmony with God’s Commandments.
So, after you’ve experienced forgiveness, the big question is—how do you move forward?
It’s not just about staying away from old mistakes. It’s about building a life that’s full of lasting peace and real joy. And here’s the heart of it: aligning your life with God’s commandments. Not because you’re scared of breaking the rules, but because you genuinely feel love and gratitude.
Picture this: a young couple, just married, trying to build their new life together. They’re hoping for a home filled with kindness, honesty, and faith. But, let’s be honest, the pressures of work, family, and day-to-day life can make it tough to focus on what matters most. Still, they make a choice—to put God’s commandments at the center. They carve out time for prayer, serve others, and always have each other’s backs.
Over time, something shifts. Their home turns into a real haven—a place that feels safe and warm, no matter how stormy life gets outside.
Now, let’s talk about obedience. It’s easy to see it as a burden, right? Just a bunch of rules holding you back. But ask anyone who’s gone through repentance and forgiveness—they’ll tell you, obedience is actually the key to happiness that lasts. It keeps you close to God, helps you steer clear of old pain, and gives your life deeper purpose.
Here’s something to remember: God doesn’t just hand out commandments at random. They’re given out of love. They’re a guide to what really brings joy. And most of us, sooner or later, find out that when we try to live by these principles, there’s a peace that shows up—a peace you just can’t find anywhere else.
Sure, life’s challenges don’t disappear, but you’ll find new strength to face them.
Of course, nobody’s immune to temptation. Old habits can pull you back, and the urge to slip up is real. When that happens, it helps to look back—remember the pain from past mistakes, the relief that came with forgiveness, and the hope that things can be better. Every single day is a fresh chance to make wiser choices and build on what you’ve already learned.
Take the story of a man who struggled with dishonesty in his business. Deciding to change wasn’t easy, especially when money was tight and the temptation to cut corners was strong. But he stuck with it. And as he did, something amazing happened—his reputation got better, his relationships grew stronger, and he started to feel a real sense of self-respect. What started as a tough effort to keep the commandments actually became a source of strength.
Living in harmony with God’s commandments doesn’t mean you have to be perfect. Everyone stumbles sometimes. What matters is that you keep trying, ask for forgiveness when you need it, and stay on the path.
The journey never really ends, but the rewards are real—a life filled with peace, purpose, and the deep assurance that you’re loved by God.

Chapter 6: Facing Persistent Weaknesses and the Struggle to Change
Have you ever felt that quiet frustration, when you try over and over to change something about yourself, but it just won’t budge? Maybe it’s a temper that flares up at exactly the wrong time. Or a habit that clings on, no matter how many promises you make to quit. Sometimes, it’s a pattern of thinking that keeps dragging you back into old regrets. At first, you hope for a quick fix—but as time passes, you realize that some weaknesses are just stubborn companions.
Let me tell you about a woman in her forties. Her friends and family respected her, but she found herself constantly wrestling with envy. She genuinely wanted to be happy for other people’s successes, but, almost every time, that little pang of resentment crept in. She prayed. She read. She tried to count her blessings. But the feeling stuck around. And every time she slipped, she couldn’t help but wonder—would she ever really change?
If we're honest, most of us have something like this—a weakness that feels like it’s woven right into who we are. The struggle can feel pretty lonely, even hopeless at times. But here’s something to pay attention to: Persistent weakness isn’t proof that you’ve failed. It’s actually a call to reach for help beyond yourself.
Getting past these deep-seated flaws? It’s rarely a straight path. There are days when you feel like you’re making progress, only to face setbacks that really sting. It’s tempting to believe that if you keep failing, maybe forgiveness is out of reach. But the truth is, God’s patience is so much bigger than most of us imagine. The willingness to keep trying, to keep turning back, matters far more than perfection ever could.
Take another example—a man haunted by a quick temper. He found himself apologizing to his family more times than he could count. Sometimes, he worried his efforts were pointless, that he’d never be free of his anger. But over time, he started to notice a few small changes: pauses before he spoke, moments when he chose to walk away instead of lashing out. The progress was slow. But it was real.
That’s when it became clear: the miracle of forgiveness isn’t just about wiping away the past. It’s about empowering real change, right here in the present. The atonement of Christ isn’t a one-time event—it’s a source of strength you can draw on again and again. Every sincere effort, every humble prayer, is met with understanding and support.
For many people, the hardest part is actually forgiving themselves for not being further along. That little voice of discouragement whispers, “You’ll never measure up.” But the real invitation is to keep moving forward—to trust that even small steps matter. This journey isn’t about arriving at perfection. It’s about becoming a little better, a little kinder, each day.

Let's dive into Chapter 7: The Challenge and Freedom of Forgiving Others.
You know, if asking for forgiveness feels tough, offering it to someone else can be even more of a struggle. The pain of betrayal, harsh words, or broken trust can sit with us for a long time. Sometimes, the hurt is so raw that the idea of letting go just feels out of reach. But here’s something to really consider—forgiveness isn’t just something we’re asked to do. It’s actually a gift we end up giving ourselves.
Picture a father who’s been distant from his adult son for years. Misunderstandings have piled up, and he carries this quiet ache wherever he goes. He replays old arguments in his mind, each one making his sense of injustice sharper. For the longest time, he thought holding onto his anger would shield him from more pain. But in reality, that anger became a heavy burden—coloring every conversation and stealing his peace.
Maybe that scenario sounds familiar. So many of us hold on to resentment, believing that forgiving someone means we’re excusing what happened, or pretending it didn’t hurt. But real forgiveness? It’s something else entirely. It’s a choice—a decision to let go of the grip that pain and anger have on our hearts. It doesn’t erase what happened, but it does open the door to healing.
Take the story of a woman who was deeply hurt by a close friend’s betrayal. For years, she just couldn’t move past it. She tried to avoid thinking about it, but that bitterness stuck around. One day, it hit her—her anger was costing her far more than the original wound ever did. She started to pray for the strength to forgive, even though she didn’t feel ready. It was slow going—some days, she felt a bit lighter, but other days, the old pain crept back in. Still, over time, her resentment loosened its hold.
Forgiving others isn’t about pretending the hurt wasn’t real. It’s about choosing not to let that pain decide what happens next in your life. And here’s the incredible part—most people discover, often to their own surprise, that forgiveness sets them free. All that energy spent nursing old wounds becomes available for new joys, new relationships, and fresh growth.
Now, there are situations where reconciliation just isn’t possible—or even safe. Some relationships are too damaged, or too risky, to mend. But even then, forgiveness is still in reach. It’s an internal release—a way to let go of the need for revenge or to be proven right.
The teachings of Christ are clear: as we forgive others, we open ourselves to receive forgiveness too. It’s not about keeping score—it’s about transformation. When we let go of anger, our hearts soften, making more space for love and peace. And maybe the real miracle is this: by forgiving others, we find our own healing.

Chapter 8: Hope for Those Who Feel Beyond Forgiveness.
You know, there’s a special kind of despair that can creep in when someone starts to believe they’ve gone too far—like their mistakes are simply too big to be forgiven.
It’s a heavy feeling, isn’t it? The book doesn’t ignore this fear. Actually, it faces it head-on, sharing real stories and gentle reassurance for anyone who feels lost in that darkness.
Picture a teenager, stuck in a cycle of bad choices. He started to believe he was beyond help. Eventually, he just stopped trying. He quit praying, convinced that even God had given up on him. The shame he carried built a wall, keeping him isolated from anyone who might want to help. But then, something remarkable happened. A trusted mentor opened up, sharing their own story of failure and redemption. Suddenly, that wall of shame started to crack.
The truth is, so many people walk around carrying secret burdens—regrets about choices they made, words they wish they could take back, opportunities that slipped by. That fear of being unworthy? It can be paralyzing. But here’s something to hold on to: at the very heart of the gospel is this message—no one is ever out of reach of Christ’s love. The atonement really is infinite. It covers every sin, every weakness, every single failure.
Think about a woman, haunted by a decision she made decades ago. For years, she believed she could never be clean again. She started avoiding church, dodged friends, and tried to bury her pain. But one quiet day, she found herself listening to a message about forgiveness. And something inside her shifted. She realized the invitation to come back was still there—she hadn’t been forgotten after all.
Of course, the journey back isn’t easy. It takes real courage to face the truth, admit you need help, and trust that forgiveness is possible. But here’s the amazing part—when someone takes that first tiny step, the way forward starts to get clearer. The burden slowly lifts, and hope takes its place.
What really stands in the way of forgiveness? Most often, it’s just the belief that it’s out of reach. But the promise is real. No matter how far someone’s wandered, the way back is always open. The invitation is simple: trust, take a step, and believe that change is possible.

Chapter 9—The Ongoing Journey: Building a Life of Forgiveness.
Forgiveness isn’t just something you do once and then move on. It’s actually a way of living, woven right into the fabric of everyday life. Sometimes, it’s those quiet, almost invisible moments—a quick apology, a gentle letting go. Other times, forgiveness shows up in big, soul-searching decisions that change how you see yourself and others.
Here’s what this book invites you to consider: Forgiveness isn’t just something you wait to receive. It’s a principle you get to practice, day in and day out.
I want you to think about a young mother—she’s juggling all the demands of parenting, and, like so many of us, sometimes she loses her patience. Each night, she promises herself she’ll do better tomorrow. But every new day brings its own challenges. What changed her home wasn’t being perfect. It was learning to say “I’m sorry” quickly, forgiving herself for the rough moments, and giving herself permission to try again. Gradually, her family learned that mistakes weren’t disasters—they were just part of being human. And in that space, everyone felt safe to start over.
Isn’t it true that the need for forgiveness never really disappears? There are always fresh mistakes, new misunderstandings, and more chances to choose grace instead of judgment. And here’s something beautiful—each time you forgive, whether you’re on the giving or receiving end, the next act of forgiveness gets just a little bit easier.
There’s another story—this time, it’s a man looking back over his life. He realized that the moments he treasured most weren’t when he nailed everything perfectly. Instead, they were those second chances, those times when someone saw past his flaws and offered a fresh start. The relationships that stuck with him were the ones where forgiveness flowed freely—where love mattered more than pride.
This journey? It doesn’t really have an end point. Some days, you’ll feel like you’re making progress. Other days, you might stumble. But choosing to build a life around forgiveness brings a deep sense of peace and purpose that lasts. It’s not about erasing what’s happened before—it’s about creating a future where hope always has room to grow.

Chapter 10: The Promise of Transformation and Lasting Peace
At the very heart of everything we've talked about is a promise—one that runs deeper than just erasing mistakes. Forgiveness, at its core, isn’t just about letting go of the past. It's about allowing yourself to become someone new.
Repentance and forgiveness, together, have the power to truly transform you. They shift the way you see yourself, the way you connect with others, and even the way you experience the world around you.
Let me share a story—one that might sound familiar. There was a man who spent years running from his past, always looking over his shoulder, weighed down by regret. One day, though, he finally found the courage to turn around and face it all. His journey wasn’t easy. There were plenty of setbacks, moments when doubt crept in, and times when he wondered if things would ever really change. But he kept going. And as he did, he discovered something incredible—a new sense of self, rooted not in shame, but in hope. The peace he found along the way ran deeper than anything he’d ever known before.
So, what’s the real promise here? It’s not that life will suddenly be free of struggle or pain. Instead, it’s knowing that no matter what happens, there’s always a way forward. The atonement of Christ offers more than just a do-over. It gives you the power to become new—to step into a life that’s filled with real hope.
The invitation is simple, but powerful: trust the process. Keep moving forward. Believe that lasting peace isn’t just possible—it’s waiting for you.
For so many people, the journey of forgiveness becomes the foundation for a life filled with service, compassion, and genuine joy. The hard lessons learned along the way? They become gifts—something you can share to help others. And the peace you find in being forgiven? It turns into a strength that lets you guide others as they try to find their own way.
That’s the real miracle of forgiveness. It’s not just about wiping the slate clean. It’s about transforming lives—yours included. No matter how far you’ve wandered, the journey is open to everyone. The invitation is always there: take the first step, trust, and discover the peace that comes from living in harmony with God, and with yourself.

As we wrap up, let’s take a moment to bring it all together. Forgiveness isn’t some quick fix or a single moment you check off a list. It’s a journey, full of ups and downs, honesty, and a willingness to keep moving forward—even when things feel slow or tough.
The stories and lessons from The Miracle of Forgiveness remind us that everybody trips up sometimes. We all struggle. And the beautiful truth is, there’s always a chance to start again.
So, what’s the real takeaway here? Forgiveness is a process—it unfolds over time. Those persistent weaknesses you notice? They’re not proof you’ve failed, but invitations to try again. When you choose to forgive, you’re not just letting someone else off the hook—you’re freeing your own heart, making space for healing.
And remember, nobody’s out of reach when it comes to Christ’s love. His atonement covers everyone. Real peace doesn’t come from just asking for forgiveness once, but by living it—day in and day out.
If regret feels heavy, or forgiveness seems out of reach, know this: you’re not alone. There’s always a way back, no matter how many detours you’ve taken. Every honest step matters—whether it’s admitting where you are, saying you’re sorry, or deciding to let go.
Sure, the path can be slow and setbacks are real, but the promise of real change is just as real. Your efforts matter. Your struggles are seen. And your hope for something better? That’s not wasted.
The miracle of forgiveness isn’t for the flawless—it’s for anyone with the courage to begin. So take heart. Take that next step. The peace you’re looking for? It’s closer than you think.
